With this number The Diamond begins its third
volume, grateful for past favors and indulgence and
hoping by strict adherence to Fraternity interests to
merit future encouragement and approval.
Although young in years, it is old in the experience
of early struggles incident to the growth of new enter
prises. Encouraged by success and learning wisdom
from mistakes, it is better prepared than ever to begin
another campaign in the precarious field of Fraternity
journalism.
For nearly half a century W. T. grew and prospered
without the aid of a magazine ; and when progress in
the Fraternity dictated a change of policy it was ex
tremely difficult for some of our conservative brothers
to become accustomed to the novelty of an organ
through which Psi U. can speak to the outside world
and yet not throw open the doors of our penetralia to
the gaze of curious eyes.
The Board has labored earnestly, and many times
with too little assistance, in the endeavor to publish a
journal worthy of the Fraternity to which we have the
honor to belong. Its success, prosperity and advance
ment will be our highest ambition.
The management of a Fraternity paper is beset with
innumerable difficulties, the bias of chapters, the es
tablished prejudice and opinions of individuals. The
entire Fraternity cannot be agreed upon every topic
of Fraternity interest. Before the pulse of the Frater
nity has been thoroughly examined, mistakes will be
made, and frequently a misguided policy will be fol
lowed for a short time.
We recognize that experience and close observation
of the needs of our organization are the elements of
journalistic success.
This number comes to our subscribers in a new
dress adorned with the ornaments peculiar to Psi
Upsilon.
The changes are the result of the increased encour
agement which our enterprise has received from all
hands, and continued support will warrant further im
provements.
We soon will have added to our Fraternity literature
one of the most valuable books of its kind ever written
�
the Epitome. The general scope of the work and
the author's ability and diligence in collecting inform
ation give us reason to believe that the Epitome will
not only satisfy but transcend our expectations.
We are in possession of a number of facts in regard
to this publication which we will take pleasure in com
municating to our readers.
From a large number of papers prepared since his
initiation into Psi Upsilon, all bearing upon different
phases of our Society's outward development, Bro.

1,000 members the announcement of a

under the title of an

Epitome."
Although at that time it was impossible to send

the book is issued. No particular rule of selection
was adopted, although circulars were addressed to
most of the recent initiates.

2 THE DIAMOND.
Fortunately the subscriptions have been so numer
ous, and the expressions of approval so general as to
justify the publication of a larger and more expensive
volume than was at first contemplated.
Bro. Jacobs informs us that "from the revered
founders of our Fraternity and from its several branches,
from judges, senators, congressmen, authors, bishops,
and college professors, men representing all the differ
ent chapters and classes, letters have been received
containing the warmest encouragement. Among the
many who have been interested in the project and
who have contributed valuable information, are the
Rev. Dr. Goodale, Judge Van Vorst, ex-Gov. Rice,
Congressman Robinson, ex-Senator Cole, Bishops Sey
mour and Perry and others equally well known. Dr.
Goodale's kindness has enabled me to procure for the
book 2. fac simile engraving of one of the original
badges."
The book will contain tables of membership, honors,
etc., complete for fifty years, ending Nov. 24, 1883.
The value of the publication as a statistical record of
the first half century of our existence cannot be com
puted.
One of the novel and interesting features of the
Epitome will be an
engraving of the building in which
the Fraternity was founded.
Although every one is anxiously awaiting the pubhcation of this volume, yet the delay is pardonable, inas
much as the author is using the time in the addition
of interesting features not contemplated in the be
ginning.
While other Fraternity papers apparently consider
their exchange department one of their most important
features, filling page after page with gratuitous gabble
about the merits or short comings of their rivals, The
Diamond has never
given any space to exchange
notices.
The interest which some of our sister societies
evince in the successes or misfortunes of others fre
quently exceeds their manifest attention to the wel
fare of their own
Fraternity.
We have never
favorably considered the introduc
tion of an
exchange department into the columns of
The Diamond, and we are confident that our course
meets the approval of the members of Psi Upsilon.
When our desire to participate in the exchange gos
sip, so prevalent with the Fraternity press, surpasses
our devotion to Psi Upsilon, we will reconsider our
course.
The garments of Psi Upsilon are not to be soiled by
entering into promiscuous exchange imbroglios started
for the amusement of every LiUputian organization that
may choose to raise a
cry.
We announce it as an established policy of The
Diamond not to exchange with any Fraternityjournal.
We do not wish to be understood as
intending
any disrespect to any of the good Fraternities, for
personality is not involved in our position. Our policy
is irrespective of any organization.
Psi Upsilon has formed her policies independent of
any Fraternity for fifty years, and will continue in the
same course for fifty years longer, as far as The Dia
mond is concerned.
Exchanging is one of the first stages of Pan-Hellenicism, with which we have no sympathy whatever.
Both ideas are incompatible with the policies of a
Fraternity that professes to be secret.
The Diamond is for Psi U's, and for Psi U's alone.
We call the attention of our readers to the account
of the organization of a Kansas Alumni Association,
given in another column.
Psi U's all over the country will unite in praising
the energy, enterprise and Fraternity spirit manifested
by those devoted members who were instrumental in
forming this Association.
It certainly gives early evidence of great activity.
An elegant little sheet has been published, containing
a list of the members of the Fraternity in Kansas,
giving their occupations and places of residence.
A private letter from a brother who was chiefly
interested in the organization of the Association, says :
"
We may be in the '
Great American Desert,' but we
are Psi Upsilons to the back-bone. Any Psi Upsilon
that may come this way can feel assured of fraternal
welcome."
We have no doubt that if any one going to Kansas
should constitute himself a committee of investigation,
he would find the statement fully in accord with the
truth.
Some of our large Psi U. centers, without an Asso
ciation, should be stimulated to action by the example
of Kansas�

SEMICENTENNIAL CONVENTION PRO
CEEDINGS.
The proceedings of the Semi-Centennial Conven
tion will be published in book or pamphlet form,
under the management of The Diamond. Owing to
the difficulty of collecting all the MSS., its publication
has been delayed.
It will contain Prof Price's Address of Welcome to
the Delegates ; Ex-Gov. Rice's Introductory Address
at the literary exercises; Senator Hawley's Oration;
Prof. Boyesen's Poem; Mr. Warner's Essay; Prof.
Harrington's Ode ; all the toasts at the banquet ; the
names of all who attended the convention, and such
other details as were connected with the event.
It will be a desirable addition to any library, both
on account of its literary worth, and also on account
of its value as a complete history of an
important
event. No expense will be spared in placing it before
the Fraternity in an attractive form.
In a few days circulars will be sent to all the mem
bers, giving the chief features of the book, the price,
time of publication, and all further necessary par
ticulars.

THE ALUMNI ASSOCIATION OF THE
NORTHWEST.
On the evening of May 25, at the time of the
Convention banquet at Albany, the Psi Upsilon Asso
ciation of the Northwest held a banquet and reception

4 THE DIAMOND.
at the Palmer House, in Chicago. On this occasion a
novel feature, in the way of an innovation, was intro
duced, consisting in the attendance of Psi Upsilon
ladies at both banquet and reception. The reception,
though somewhat limited in the number present, by
reason of the inclemency of the weather, was, never
theless a brilliant one and most heartily enjoyed by
all who were present. The parlor floor and the large
ball-room of the hotel were given up to the occasion.
After an hour of music and sociability, the party re
paired to the ordinary of the hotel where a bounteous
repast was laid. The tables were handsomely deco
rated, the floral display and the menu cards and
dancing programmes being the subject of much favor
able comment. The menu was disposed of, inter
larded with the retelling of college and fraternity
anecdotes, the singing of the old songs, and frequent
selections rendered by the orchestra present. Tele
grams were exchanged with the convention at Albany,
and with various Psi Upsilons. The usual toasts and
responses were indulged in, many of the latter being
pithy and worthy of mention. Among those present
and responding were : Hon. Bro. John T. Wentworth,
President of the Association ; Judge Henry Booth,
Beta, '40 ; C. M. Fay, Psi, '62 ; R. L. Dakin, Psi, '53 ;
Hon. William H. Barnes, Phi, '68 ; H. A. Coohdge,
Zeta, '49. Letters were read from Bros. President
Angell, Profs. George S. Morris, Charles K. Adams,
E. L. Walter, and others. After the banquet, an ad
journment was had to the ball-room, where to the
music of Frieberg's large and excellent orchestra the
numbers on the dancing programme were observed
and the company did not disperse until an early
hour in the morning.

PSI UPSILON association.
One of the most distinctive and important features
of American colleges is the system of secret societies.
These organizations seem to have been coeval with the
coUeges themselves, and within the past half century
have grown so strong and become so prominent that
they must be considered as one of the great institu
tions of this country. These societies are more secret
in their nature and far more fraternal in the relations
of the members one with another than the various
secret organizations of the world at large, though not
so complicated and extensive in their structure. The
name of each of these societies is composed of two
or three letters of the Greek alphabet, which stand
for as many Greek words, comprising the motto that
indicates the purposes, aims or actions of the society ;
these words are unknown to all, except the initiates of
the society. These societies have lodges, or chapters,
as they are styled, in the principal colleges of the
country. These chapters are variously designated, but
all bear the common name of the fraternity and are
subject to a general governing body, which each chap
ter has a voice in electing. The benefits and advan
tages of these organizations are incalculable, especially
while in college, and the friendships and associations
therein formed are
among the dearest and most lasting
of one's entire life.
One of the oldest and probably the strongest and
best college fraternity in existence is Psi Upsilon. It
was founded at Union College, Schenectady, N. Y., in
1833, and since then has placed chapters in eighteen
of the leading colleges of the country. It has no
chapters in the obscure colleges of the South and
West, and is the only fraternity which has but one
inactive chapter. Its chapter houses and temples rep
resent an expenditure of nearly $100,000, and this is
being steadily increased by the further acquisition of
property. Members of Psi Upsilon are to be found
occupying positions of honor and trust in both public

THE DIAMOND. 5
and business life. The President of the United States
is an honored and enthusiastic member of the Fra
ternity, having united with it when a student in Union
College, from which institution he graduated in 1848.
Such is the organization which is now represented
in this State by the Kansas Alumni Association of
Psi Upsilon, which was formed in this city last Thurs
day. Most of the large cities have similar associations,
but this is the first State Alumni Association ever
formed and the only one of any Fraternity in Kansas.
Such organizations are formed for the mutual enjoy
ment of the members, the renewal of old and precious
memories and the promotion of the interests of the
Fraternity at large.
The officers of the Kansas Association for the first
term are as follows : President, D. M. Swan, of Leav
enworth ; First Vice-President, Rev. Abiel Leonard, of
Atchison; Second Vice-President, Judge James H.
Austin, of Junction City ; Secretary and Treasurer,
Bestor G. Brown, of Topeka.
The next meeting of the association will be held in
May, either in Topeka or Atchison, as may hereafter
be decided.

The chapter rooms of the Delta are situated on
Broadway, near the College, and afford a convenient
place for the members to drop in, either before or
after recitations, and spend their spare time in conver

library, containing books on almost every subject
studied in the University. Our meetings are held
weekly, and are attended, not only by the active
members, but also the graduates, and those of the
Faculty, who are Psi U's. By means of a
legacy
left by an early graduate of the chapter, the ex

we initiate no one to our chapter until he has been a
regular matriculate of the University for three months,
feeling sure that a less time is insufficient to learn all
we should of a man whom we are to make our most
intimate friend, not only for the four years he is in

The semi-centennial disposed of, our breth
ren returned to routine work with a feeling of relief,
and we enter upon the second half century of the
parent Chapter's existence with considerable satisfac
tion with the record of the past fifty years, and with
bright anticipations for the future. We have initiated
our share of good men from the new matriculants, and
in numbers are still ariiong the first in Union. With
the graduation of '83 we lost several respected and
loyal brothers, active workers in the interests of the
Fraternity. The withdrawal of Bro. McCauley, '85,
removes from the Chapter a
genial companion, and
from the College a famous athlete. We still maintain
our grip upon College honors. A neutral was the
"
crome
"
at our last commencement, but our senior
delegation was represented by two orators, and the
two junior essay prizes were awarded respectively to
Bros. Beekman and Allison. Our brethren hold the
presidencies of the canoe and athletic associations and
several of the minor offices, as well as prominent
places in the classes and hterary societies. We still
cling to our old rooms, but are looking forward eager
ly to the time not far distant when our Chapter house
will be a reality. We are hopeful now that it will be
the first society building in this College, with the ex
ception of that interesting relic and peculiar piece of
antique furniture known as the "
Sig. Cheese Box."
For the first time in many years has a shadow been
cast over our Chapter life. In July last, died at his
home in Schenectady, of consumption, after a yea,r's
illness, Albert Moore Westinghouse, '83. Brother
Westinghouse was a nephew of the inventor of the
Westinghouse air-brakes. He was a man of unusual

ability, and of a sociable nature that endeared him
personally to all of his associates. Even in his
sickness he desired to entertain the members of the
Chapter at his home. He was a man of whom great
deeds were anticipated, both on account of his perse
vering application and his natural and inherited genius.
His Fraternity life had always been marked by his zeal

Theta indebted for many generous and disinterested
services. Upon the reassembling of the Chapter this
term the vacancy in our midst was deeply felt, and
with sorrowful hearts did we pay our last tribute to the
memory of our affectionate and beloved companion.

The University of Chicago, in which our
Chapter has been established since 1869, has been
laboring for some years under a peculiar combination
of circumstances. Many years ago the trustees of the
University borrowed ^75,000, for what purpose is not
now definitely known, but certain it is that no part of
the debt or accumulated interest was ever paid until
within the last five years. The property was be
queathed by the late Stephen A. Douglas for the pur
poses of an educational institution, the conditions of
the will being that in case the property be no longer
used for an educational institution it should revert to
the Douglas heirs. The question which now arises is
"
to whom will the property revert in case the insur
ance company now holding the mortgage should fore
close ?
"
By virtue of foreclosure it would go to the in
surance company, while by virtue of the will it would
go to the Douglas heirs. Money can be easily raised
in this city to pay off the original indebtedness, or to
endow the University, when once it shall be freed
fi-om debt, but objections to paying compound interest
are of course advanced. Through the efforts of Dr.
Anderson, a proposition looking towards a
compromise
has been advanced, and will probably in the near
future be realized. The public confidence in the ex
cellent management of Dr. Anderson is amply evinced
by the largely increased attendance of the University,
there being this year over twice as
many students as
were in attendance two years ago. The acquisitions
have been almost wholly to the preparatory depart-
'
ment, but the men have staying qualities.
The Fraternities have all suffered more or less from
the extreme paucity of eligible men in the last few
years, but the standard of Psi U. has been maintained
to the last, and we will preserve that standard if there
be not a man left in the Chapter. But there is no
reason why the Omega should not make rapid strides
toward rivaling the eastern Chapters in numbers. We
have at present an ideal Chapter. Though small in
number, we are a fraternal body in every sense of the

evinced by the large number of pledged men we have

The Omega has undoubtedly passed through a con
tinued series of hardships in the last year, but this year
bids fair to present nothing but plain sailing, and by
next year we shall have a large and politically strong
Chapter. The reason that we have in the past few
years had so few men was because of our rigid adher
ence to the conservative W. T. policy, and this, as I
have stated, we intend to maintain.
Our Chapter is the nucleus of a large northwestern
alumni association, and our movements are commend
ed by that body. There must be a Chapter here, and
we feel that we must maintain it in accordance with
the well established reputation of W. F. in general. We
are fully confident that the course of time will obliter
ate all prejudices against the University. We deny
that there are any just prejudices against the Omega.
